items.good: The README has the template's headings in its order: the name, an opening under no heading, Example, Why tidy-downloads, Requirements, Installation, Documentation, Development, License. The opening's first sentence gives the idea (it shows every move first, never deletes, renames, overwrites or changes a file, and can put the last move back). The next sentences give the gain, the kind of thing that gives it (a command typed in a terminal) and whom it is for. Installation ends with the first use, pointing to the Example. Each Why and Requirements item is one sentence that reads on its own, with any explanation after a blank line and indented. No item is in bold.

From the opening I can tell this is for me if I use macOS or Linux, type commands in a terminal and have a Downloads folder that fills up. I also learn what sets it apart: it sorts the files in my Downloads, or another folder I name, into folders by kind, shows every move before making it, never overwrites, and can undo the last move. And I learn what I gain: I open the folder for a file's kind in place of searching one long list.

The example uses a Downloads folder like mine. It names the files, including one with no extension and one whose name is taken in a folder I made earlier. It then shows, in the order I would do them, the preview, the move and the undo, each with the exact output the tool prints. It ends at the result: where the photo now is, which folders were made, and the state after undo. So I can picture running it on my own Downloads.

Each point in Why is set against sorting by hand or against a script of mv commands: one command in place of dragging each file, a preview in place of moving as it runs, a file never moved onto one of the same name where mv would overwrite it, and one-command undo where a file manager takes back one drag at a time. No benefit that every way gives is placed among or before these.

parts.good: I take in the opening on one reading. 'Folder named for its kind' is shown in the same paragraph by Images, Documents and Archives. Each promise is said in full, and whom it is for is said directly.

The starting state is set out before the first command. Each command and its output is in a block to copy. Other is explained right under the output where it first appears, and so is why invoice.pdf stays. After each block comes what is now true, including that files inside folders stay and that a second undo moves nothing. Sorting another folder is shown as commands in a block.
Each point names what tidy-downloads does and what the other way does in its place, and every case named (a file of the same name, undo) says what happens. Nothing rests on a later part.

Each requirement says what it is and how I tell whether I have it: python3 --version prints a version, and curl comes with macOS and most Linux systems. It also says where to get each one I lack: python.org or any way I like, and a web browser in place of curl.

The install steps come in order as blocks to copy. The other-folder case and the no-curl case each say what to do. The check comes in a block, and if the check fails, the README says how to find the shell and which line to add for each case: zsh, bash on Linux, bash on macOS. Then I am pointed to the first use.
Both places are named in one reading: --help for every way to run it, and the commit history with its address for changes.
One line says where a builder starts and gives the link.
The license is named in one sentence.

items.good: Each part gives me something no other part does. The opening gives the promises. The Example shows them on files with real output and adds what it alone tells: Other, folders being made, files in subfolders staying, a second undo moving nothing, and the command for another folder. Why adds what the hand and mv ways do in place of each promise. Requirements and Installation add only what I need to get it running, and Installation points back to the Example rather than repeating it. Nothing is addressed to a reviewer, tells how a decision was reached, or gives fuller use.
